newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azeris stop retransmission of Iranian television.
newsitem.headline: Azeris stop retransmission of Iranian television.

text.p: Azerbaijan, in a sign of worsening ties with Iran, has stopped daily retransmission of Iranian television programmes over what it says is "interference in its internal politics" and "one-sided propaganda" by Tehran.
Azerbaijani television had retransmitted an hour of Azeri-language news from Iran daily across the former Soviet republic of eight million for the last two years.
But the midday broadcasts on the main state channel, usually anchored by a woman in a traditional Moslem headscarf, abruptly disappeared from television screens this week.

Mamedali Zulfugarov, acting director of Azerbaijan's television, told the government newspaper Khalg (Nation) that the broadcasts had formed part of an exchange accord under which Iranian television broadcast Azerbaijani-made programmes.
"Unfortunately, Azerbaijani television programmes have not been shown in Iran recently," Zulfugarov said.
"The agreement says that the programmes will not interfere in each others' internal politics and will not involve one-sided propaganda. The Iranian broadcasts ignored those conditions."
He disputed a claim in one Iranian broadcast that 16 Azerbaijani regions spoke the Iranian Farsi language rather than the Turkic Azeri tongue.
The two Caspian Sea countries share a long frontier while at least 14 million ethnic Azeris are estimated to live in Iran, mostly in northwestern provinces which border Azerbaijan.
A duty officer reached by telephone at the Iranian embassy in Baku said no one was available for comment.
Despite common Shi'ite Moslem roots, the two countries have embarked on radically different political paths.

Azerbaijan, under President Haydar Aliyev, has chosen a strongly secular, pro-Western model of development reinforced by 70 years of officially atheist Soviet rule which ended with the collapse of the empire in 1991.
Baku, developing huge offshore oil resources, has accused Tehran in the past of wanting to overthrow its government and replace it with a conservative Islamic pro-Iranian one.
Four members of Azerbaijan's banned Islamic party were given long prison terms this year for allegedly spying for Tehran.
Zulfugarov said it was possible that a new agreement could be found to provide for Iranian broadcasting in Azerbaijan but that Tehran would have to guarantee it would be non-political.
